weaknesses: The theoretical justification has substantive errors. Theorem 2 assumes output proximity for the given input, but Appendix B.2 derives closeness of value-projection matrices by assuming proximity for all possible single-token inputs. That stronger assumption is unstated; different value projections can compensate for different attention matrices while producing identical outputs. The proof also replaces approximate sparsity with exact sparsity without a residual term. Appendix B.3 additionally uses a false spectral-norm contraction claim for row-stochastic attention matrices. These issues undermine the claimed rigorous connection between output and attention similarity.

The accuracy–efficiency tradeoff is not evaluated under matched configurations. Appendix D.1 uses draft generation until EOS for SpecKV accuracy, but fixes lookahead to 64 tokens for timing. Moreover, Figure 6 attributes the speedup to sparse prefill without comparing against SnapKV combined with the same sparse-prefill machinery. TTFT measurements alone do not establish the abstract's throughput claims.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. SpecKV changes attention reduction from mean to max alongside adding lookahead, without a corresponding no-lookahead/max-reduction control. For default SpecPC, n_lookahead=1 means its attention tensor contains only prompt queries under the stated indexing. Its principal results therefore demonstrate small-model attention transfer, rather than the advertised use of generated future-token information.

Budget and reporting inconsistencies limit reproducibility. Algorithm 2 selects Cmax non-window tokens and then adds the window, yielding Cmax+n_window tokens rather than the stated total budget. It is unclear whether experiments follow the algorithm or prose. Table 9 also reports 48.46 for Ada-SpecKV at budget 512, whereas its category scores imply approximately 47.04 under the stated task averaging. The promised code URL is absent from the supplied manuscript.

Important comparisons are missing or altered. HeadKV and LongLLMLingua are discussed but not evaluated. Appendix D.2 changes H2O and StreamingLLM to one-time post-prefill eviction, so these results do not evaluate their original decoding-time policies. These choices weaken the broad state-of-the-art claim.

The attention-correlation evidence does not establish reliable importance transfer. Aggregated correlation across layers, heads, queries, and tokens can conceal poor agreement on the tokens actually retained. Figure 8 reports mean R²=0.00 for the main Qwen pair and max R²=0.03–0.07 for Gemma pairs. Per-example ranking agreement, top-k overlap, and analyses excluding attention sinks would better test the proposed explanation.

Generality and consistent-superiority claims exceed the evidence. Larger-model experiments use only 50 examples per task without uncertainty estimates, and the six multimodal datasets were selected partly for large draft–target performance gaps. There are also clear reversals: in Table 12 at budget 1024, SnapKV scores 48.46 versus 47.52 and 48.15 for the two SpecKV configurations. These limitations should be reflected in the conclusions.

The reported results show promising practical gains. On Llama-70B, SpecKV-PC achieves 51.60 on LongBench versus 48.43 for LAQ++ at the same stated final cache budget. The H200 experiments include draft overhead and demonstrate substantial latency and memory savings for the cascaded method.

The draft-size, lookahead-length, sparse-prefill, and importance-correlation analyses provide useful empirical insight into when the methods work, including experiments on longer summarization outputs.
weaknesses: Theorem 2 is not valid under its stated assumptions. Appendix B.2 derives a bound on the difference between value projections by switching to a one-token input and quantifying over arbitrary inputs, although the theorem only assumes output closeness for the given input. Different value projections can compensate for different attention matrices, yielding identical outputs without identical attention. The proof also treats approximate sparsity as exact sparsity without a residual term. Separately, Theorem 3’s proof incorrectly assumes that a row-stochastic attention matrix contracts the matrix spectral norm. These are substantive problems in a claimed theoretical contribution.

Several aggregate scores contradict the stated averaging procedure. With category task counts of 3, 3, 3, 3, and 2, Table 9’s PyramidKV result at Cmax=1024 implies an overall score of 45.85, rather than 48.31. Table 12’s Ada-SpecKV result at Cmax=512 implies 47.04, rather than 48.46. These discrepancies exceed rounding error and can affect rankings; the tables and underlying per-task results require an audit.

The accuracy–efficiency comparisons need better control. SpecKV generates drafts until EOS for accuracy evaluation, whereas LAQ++ uses eight lookahead tokens; the main latency evaluation instead fixes SpecKV’s lookahead to 64. Appendix E.7 adds longer-output timings but does not establish a matched accuracy–latency frontier. Matched-lookahead and matched-cost comparisons would clarify the contribution of the draft model itself. H2O is also evaluated with a modified, one-time post-prefill eviction policy rather than its original dynamic policy.

Theorem 1 has a weak connection to the implemented method and its empirical validation. It bounds mean attention under a maximum, token-aligned embedding error, while Equation 2 measures distance between sequence centroids, which can conceal large individual errors. The implementation uses maximum aggregation. Consequently, the reported centroid correlation does not validate the theorem’s assumptions or establish preservation of the selected cache entries.

Novelty is incremental relative to the acknowledged predecessors. SpecPrefill already uses a small model’s lookahead attention for prompt compression, while LAQ++ already uses lookahead for KV selection. SpecPC introduces several modifications, but the experiments do not isolate window reweighting, skipped layers, pooling, and position reassignment. A cascade using existing compression methods would also help establish what is distinctive about SpecKV-PC.

Claims of consistent superiority are stronger than the evidence. Table 2’s SpecKV improvements over LAQ++ are only 0.27 and 0.37 points, and SpecPC improves over SpecPrefill by 0.07 on Llama-70B. Only 50 examples per task are used for the main evaluation, without confidence intervals or paired significance analysis. There are also clear counterexamples: Table 13 reports lower SpecKV scores than LAQ++ at every tested cache budget.

Important reproducibility and budget ambiguities remain. Algorithm 2 selects Cmax non-window tokens and then adds all window tokens, apparently exceeding the advertised prompt budget. Algorithm 1 specifies average pooling while Table 6 specifies max pooling. Section 5.1 names a Qwen-14B target whereas the main results use Qwen-32B. The promised public-code link is not identifiable in the supplied manuscript. These inconsistencies need resolution before the fixed-budget comparisons can be independently verified.

Novelty and attribution need stronger controls. SpecPC explicitly extends SpecPrefill through window weighting, pooling, and layer skipping, but these additions are not individually ablated. SpecKV uses drafts extending to EOS while LAQ++ retains an eight-token lookahead, alongside other aggregation and prefill differences. Matched controls and accuracy-versus-cost comparisons are needed to establish which changes produce the gains. Main accuracy and latency measurements also use different draft-length policies; the appendix timing sweeps only partially address this.

Claims of consistent superiority exceed the evidence. For example, Table 13 reports SpecKV below LAQ++ at all three cache budgets on Llama-3.1-8B. Several other reported LongBench improvements are small, while the main evaluation uses only 50 examples per task and supplies no confidence intervals or paired uncertainty analysis.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite substantial implementation detail. Section 5.1 identifies Qwen2.5-14B as the target, whereas the main figures and tables identify 32B. The reproducibility statement promises a public code link, but no link to the proposed implementation is identifiable in the manuscript. These inconsistencies matter particularly because LAQ++ is independently reimplemented and some baseline eviction behavior is modified.

strengths: SpecKV offers a useful practical contribution: an external draft model supplies lookahead queries without requiring LAQ++’s full target KV cache. Combining this with sparse prefill and cascaded prompt compression is promising.
RULER results show substantial improvements over relevant baselines, particularly at aggressive compression budgets and longer contexts, across Qwen and Llama models.

The experimental coverage is extensive, including multiple model sizes, compression budgets, cross-family drafts, multimodal tasks, AdaKV integration, and ablations of draft quality, lookahead length, and prefill sparsity.

The reported latency and memory reductions are practically meaningful, especially for SpecKV-PC. Pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and stage-level timing breakdowns provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification has substantive errors. Theorem 2’s proof derives a bound on the difference between value projections by assuming output closeness for arbitrary one-token inputs, whereas the theorem only states closeness for the given input. Different value projections can compensate for different attention matrices, producing identical outputs without identical attention. The proof also replaces approximate sparsity with exact sparsity without a residual term. Theorem 3 additionally relies on the false claim that every row-stochastic attention matrix contracts the matrix spectral norm.

Several reported aggregate scores contradict the averaging procedure in Section C.1. For example, Table 9’s PyramidKV results at capacity 512 imply an overall score of 44.07 from the category scores and task counts, but report 46.55; at capacity 1024, they imply 45.85 but report 48.31. Table 11’s LAQ++ result at capacity 512 similarly implies approximately 46.69 rather than 49.08. These discrepancies require correction and verification before the comparisons are reliable.

The fixed-budget comparison is ambiguous. Algorithm 2 selects Cmax tokens from outside the retained window and then adds all window tokens, yielding Cmax + nwindow tokens rather than the advertised Cmax. With the default window, this adds 64 tokens. The implementation and actual retained lengths must be clarified to establish equal-budget comparisons.

Accuracy and efficiency results are not fully aligned. SpecKV generates drafts until EOS for accuracy experiments, while LAQ++ receives eight lookahead tokens and the main latency evaluation caps SpecKV at 64. Matched-horizon controls and joint accuracy–latency–memory measurements using identical configurations are needed. Controls combining existing compression methods with sparse prefill would also better isolate the proposed method’s efficiency contribution.

Novelty beyond LAQ++ and SpecPrefill is narrower than the framework presentation suggests. SpecPC mainly changes window weighting, aggregation, layer selection, and pooling. The ablations do not isolate these changes, and the cascade lacks straightforward controls such as SpecPC followed by SnapKV. Consequently, the source and necessity of the improvements remain insufficiently established.

Claims of consistent superiority exceed the evidence. On Llama-70B LongBench, SpecPC improves over SpecPrefill by only 0.07 points, while Table 13 shows SpecKV below LAQ++ at all three cache budgets for Llama-8B. With only 50 examples per task in the main evaluation and no uncertainty estimates, small gains are inconclusive. The promising RULER results do not resolve these concerns about broader effectiveness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important inference bottleneck. Using a small draft model for KV selection offers a practical way to avoid LAQ++'s full-target-cache requirement, and combining prompt compression with KV dropping is useful.

The evaluation covers multiple Qwen and Llama models, several compression budgets, RULER and LongBench, and additional cross-family and multimodal experiments. Ablations examine draft quality, lookahead length, and prefill sparsity.

The reported RULER improvements are substantial in several aggressive-compression settings. Efficiency measurements include draft overhead, and the appendix extends timing experiments to longer outputs.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification has substantive errors. Theorem 2 assumes output closeness for the given input, but its proof derives a bound on value-weight differences by assuming closeness for arbitrary single-token inputs. This stronger assumption is unstated; different value projections can produce identical outputs despite different attention matrices. Theorem 3 also incorrectly treats row-stochastic attention as a contraction in spectral norm. These issues undermine a claimed central contribution.

Theorem 1 does not establish the practical method's reliability. It bounds mean attention under aligned, token-wise embedding errors, whereas the algorithm uses max aggregation and the empirical analysis substitutes a distance between sequence centroids. Centroid distance does not control the theorem's assumed error, and the analysis provides no guarantee for selected-token retention or downstream accuracy.

Several reported aggregate scores contradict the stated averaging procedure. With category task counts of 3, 3, 3, 3, and 2, Table 9's Qwen-32B PyramidKV row at Cmax=1024 averages to 45.85, not 48.31. Table 11's Qwen-72B LAQ++ row at Cmax=1024 averages to approximately 46.50, not 49.59. These discrepancies exceed rounding error and can reverse method rankings; the tables require reconciliation against per-task results.

Accuracy and efficiency comparisons are not fully controlled. SpecKV's accuracy evaluation generates drafts until EOS, while LAQ++ uses eight lookahead tokens and the main SpecKV timing experiment uses 64. The extended timing analysis is helpful, but does not establish a matched accuracy–latency comparison across these settings. Additionally, the H2O implementation replaces its original dynamic eviction with one-time post-prefill dropping.

The conceptual novelty is limited by the acknowledged proximity to LAQ++ and SpecPrefill. SpecPC primarily changes window weighting, aggregation, pooling, and layer selection, but these changes are not separately ablated. The experiments therefore do not clearly establish which additions account for its improvements over SpecPrefill.

Important implementation details are inconsistent. Algorithm 2 selects Cmax non-window tokens and then adds all window tokens, exceeding the stated total prompt budget. Section 5.1 identifies a 14B Qwen target, whereas the main results use 32B. These ambiguities impede reproduction and verification of fixed-budget comparisons.

The claims of consistently superior performance are stronger than the evidence. For example, Table 13 reports lower overall scores for SpecKV than LAQ++ at all three KV budgets. LongBench uses only 50 examples per task without uncertainty estimates, leaving the reliability of smaller improvements unresolved. Promising empirical results do not outweigh the theoretical and numerical problems in the current submission.

strengths: Addresses an important inference bottleneck with a practical, training-free approach. Using a separate draft model for KV selection avoids LAQ++’s requirement to retain the full target KV cache, and cascaded prompt/KV compression is a useful systems contribution.

The experimental coverage is substantial: RULER, LongBench, multiple model sizes and compression budgets, cross-family drafts, multimodal tasks, and ablations covering draft quality, lookahead length, and sparse prefill.

The reported RULER improvements under aggressive compression are promising. Efficiency measurements include draft overhead and stage-level breakdowns; the cascaded method reports substantial latency reductions and approximately 25 GB lower peak memory than LAQ++ at 64K context.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification contains substantive errors. Theorem 2 assumes output closeness for the given input, but Appendix B.2 switches to single-token inputs and assumes closeness for every input vector to bound the difference between value matrices. This stronger assumption is unstated; different attention matrices and value projections can produce identical outputs even when X satisfies RIP. The proof also replaces approximate sparsity with exact sparsity without a residual term. Appendix B.3 incorrectly asserts that a row-stochastic attention matrix contracts the spectral norm. These issues undermine a stated central contribution.

Several LongBench aggregate scores contradict the averaging rule in Appendix C.1. For example, Table 2’s Qwen-32B target categories imply 47.10 rather than 47.78, and its Llama SpecPrefill categories imply 47.45 rather than 48.37. In Table 11, LAQ++ at Cmax=1024 implies 46.50 rather than 49.59, reversing its reported ordering against SpecKV. Corrected tables and per-task results are necessary to establish reliable comparisons.

Fixed-budget and accuracy–efficiency comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Algorithm 2 selects Cmax non-window tokens and then adds the window tokens, exceeding the advertised prompt budget. SpecKV accuracy uses draft generation through EOS, whereas headline timing caps lookahead at 64 tokens; LAQ++ uses eight. Actual retained token counts and jointly measured accuracy/latency curves under identical configurations are needed.

The conceptual framework substantially overlaps with LAQ++ and SpecPrefill. SpecPC introduces window weighting, layer exclusion, pooling, and positional changes, but their individual contributions are not isolated. Despite useful existing ablations, comparisons against straightforward alternative cascades, such as SpecPrefill followed by SnapKV, are missing.

Claims of consistent superiority exceed the evidence. For example, Table 13 shows SpecKV below LAQ++ at all three KV budgets, and cross-family SpecPC degrades substantially in Table 7. Evaluation uses only 50 examples per task without confidence intervals, leaving the significance of small LongBench improvements unresolved.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistent configuration descriptions: Section 5.1 specifies a Qwen-14B target while the main results use 32B, and the main versus extended timing sections specify different draft sizes. The reproducibility statement promises public code, but the submitted manuscript provides no identifiable implementation link.
